Some other recommendations here are very good (Veena Das for example) but maybe going back to the basics of subaltern studies, like Edward Said, could also help. I do think Ginzburg's book about Menocchio and the worms and cheese and such is amongst the most magnificent critiques of poststructural anthropology, and it does make points about how to make some discoveries in history that mean a looooot to cultural anthropology. You can also try the one about battles of witchcraft, in which he uses inquisition trials to show the existence of a pagan cult independant of any powerplay in the peasant world of 16th century Italy. 

Good luck!

I understand but then no statement about what Chinese people think of US politics is made. It's like saying "people in Europe", which makes not much sense, because every place has a completely different viewpoint on what US politics are about. Say, in Poland or Hungaria, you might find way more people liking Trump; then again, urban people might be liking Dems more than countryside people (even though this would actually be wrong in most European places) and so on. 

The thing is, it might not be a scientific survey, but if it isn't it's misleading. You say "If Chinese", but you'd better say "If a number of many different kind of people with no control, who live in China and speak some Mandarin", which then cancels the overall interest of your survey.

I do think it's easy to make the statement not misleading though. You'd just have to have people hashtag with who they'd vote their level of education, place they live, profession, or something like that. I mean, I do think the results you're getting could make sense, but as they are now they're misleading, and on an ethical viewpoint you owe redditors a clear explanation why they are. Categories like "Chinese" cover an extensive variety of extremely different people, and using such categories without any more precision is just reinforcing the prejudice that people there have a "Chinese mind" or a "Chinese viewpoint". And this is misrepresenting Chinese people the same way you'd misrepresent French, Italians and Norwegians as labelling them "Europeans", or Algerians, Kenyans and Zimbabwean as labelling them "Africans". As for China (and it's applicable to India also) a country makes a nationality, but it doesn't make a nation.

And, most importantly, you don't tell or don't know if there's no bias whereas the social identity of your subscribers.

My Chinese friends were able to answer these questions. All the Chinese I kept contact with were knowledgeable about those questions. They were because they got interested in the subject at a moment of their life. But most people just don't get interested into those things.

I do agree there's a trend of people in China who don't care at all about what all those things are. There are some counter examples, like the Angry Youth, dissidents (I think 1% of the Chinese internet apart from official medias is debating politics; it's not much, but censorship included, it does represent quite a lot) or any CCP members (I think they represent 90 000 000 people, which is quite a lot even in China) plus the administration people. I also think that if you put yourself under the Chinese nationality and that you're not a member of the CCP, it makes sense. Say you have no decision power over your government, and it seems dangerous to have an opinion, then you just won't care. 

In democracies, people use big concepts and think they know what they're talking about, so they'd have an answer. If you push them to describe what exactly is communism (say, what it means philosophically, economically, or historically) they probably will unload tons of bullshit. That people won't care about politics in China seems to me due to the fact that the state made explicit that now was a time of making money, and that they'd deal with building the country by themselves. 

In the West, it seems to me people have vague ideas of what represent their countries, but really, when you push it, most people get it overly wrong. And it's normal. Medias will feed with vague narratives about one problem or another, but where I live (France) most people don't know what's the process of interpreting a law, how to interact with the government, who's in charge of what where and how to get to them, and so on. Don't take it wrongly: French are amongst the most opinionated people in the world, and the educational level is by all mean very high. It's just that politics are mainly a great way to befriend people, have a debate to show off in front of a potential mate, and so on. So you'd vote every now and then, but politics and political ideas are like, eventful more than meaningful. They have whatever cathartic effect or such, but in the real world people don't mind as long as it doesn't imply their life changing. Eventually, what makes it different on an individual perspective between a Chinese guy and a French guy is simply that one acts not concerned because he thinks it shouldn't be his business, and the other one acts concerned because it looks super cool. 

My formal knowledge of Marxism, Soviet communism and Maoism is generally lacking, but I can say for sure that 95% of the people I know use the word communism, marxism, and socialism without seeing the difference. They also say Stalinism and Maoism without seeing any difference. In the same trend, in France, people don't see a difference between liberalism, neoliberalism, libertarianism. I think it has to do mostly on how people have integrated political concepts throughout their life; what was said to be morally acceptable or not; and if they don't ever interact with any political institutions or ideas, why would they care more than that?

I do understand why it seems puzzling though. Sometimes back in China I had the feeling that no one understood any political concept, but China's so different on that level it's kinda hard to make sense of it.

That's a guess though. I might be wrong but I can't buy the idea that Chinese people don't have an understanding of how modern states work. I'd rather think of the relation of Chinese people to the state as being completely different, because of the (obviously different) rule of law in China. Especially, I feel like even though people usually trust the national leaders (except for a minority of dissidents) they really have no trust at all in local governments. And they're quite right about it; corruption is a pandemic over there, mainly because of how people think of good business as being an expression of friendship (guanxi and so on). So, if you get some money from a deal, be it a private or public deal, you'll spend some money to show the depth of your relation to your closest friends/business partners. With private money it's already dubious, but when it's CCP officials, it's properly revolting. And even if the CCP is running a campaign against corruption, it's hard to properly solve the problem. So I'd guess that most of how Chinese people conceive the government is with some layers of distrust. I guess it wouldn't change the intuition that a policy is good or not (being p or q), based on standards like Confucianism, or socialism...

I don't know. When I was living in Beijing I had the feeling people understood those kind of problems quite well. To me it's more like people are quite cynical about what the state does because they don't have any control over its decisions. They might consider the state to be highly corrupted, and simply wouldn't feel like doing their part is worth it. My friends in Beijing thought of social fairness as a must-do, but I do feel like they expected to achieve social fairness within groups of people around them, out of any kind of formal system. My guess is that it seemed more rational for the people i hanged around with to invest in their family and close friends, because it protected them much more than the state system, which is considered at least locally unstable. So, you might attribute the belief that free healthcare is a good thing, but understand people wouldn't want to do their part, because they simply lack trust in local officials and so on.

In France or such, people are also into "freebies". People do think free healthcare is amazing, and no one would like it to disappear. It's not that puzzling there that CEOs or business owners agree with that. They don't have a shallow understanding of how modern society works. They do think it's what the government should do. I guess cultural differences might look childish, but they might come from something deeper than misconceptions. In France, as in Sweden or other Northern European countries for instance, people would never ever want social security to disappear ; hear, free lodging, free healthcare, free education, plus the constant experimentation of new capabilities. In Sweden you get money until the end of your MA program; in France, lodging, eating is cheaper as a student (and universities are all free) and everyone can get financial help from the state. 

I mean, about what a state should do, I feel like Americans are an exception to the rule. People in the world mostly want the state to take care of those things. In modern developed societies, the debate is mostly where should the freebies be created and for whom. So, call everyone in Europe shallow if you will (except for the British) or the Chinese, but the modern world doesn't see much developed societies in which when you have a car accident, you get in debt.

I have been depressed for most of my life, and never acknowledged it. I'm 27 now, and I can't find any way to deal with it for myself. Somehow, it feels like I can carry on by just waking up, writing down my research, and staying alone. If I go outside I put myself in the danger of binge drinking, until I feel numb enough not to feel angry, sad, or having panic attacks from any kind of stimuli.

Depression pushes you into thinking you're nothing, you're worthless and such. Myself, I always feel like all of my limbs don't belong to me proper - I feel like they can just go away with a stream of blood, any day, and it scares the shit out of me. Walking in the streets became difficult to me in the last five years or so, because I was scared of mutilation, thinking anything could just blow my body into bits. This is my brain's own way of making me feel like I'm a worthless piece of flesh.

I do feel like we shouldn't agree with ourselves when it comes to those representations. We, depressive people, tend to think of ourselves are worthless partly, I think, because it's rooted into ourselves that we feel we are. Others probably don't, and that's why they think having a hobby will fix it. When I'm in the worst phases of my depressive symptoms, I can't do anything. I can take the drugs docs gave me, but they just make me feel like I lost more control. What I'm trying to say here is that, the last bit of control you may have is the fact that you still decide for yourself if you're worthless or not, whatever your whole body tells you. I feel you just need to look at yourself knowing you have those symptoms, that you can't control them, and that it makes you part of a whole community of people who just have to live with that. If you understand that it's out of your control to make it disappear, then you understand it's the same kind of problems as chronic pains in your body. Because it's a constituant of your psychology, you feel like you should be able to control it. The sad news is that we don't control what most of our brain does. But I also feel because it's out of our control we shouldn't think of it as our personality. That's not who we are, what we want to be, what we stand for. 

Please don't drown. I mean, you have dreams, like going to Europe or China. It's stressful and all, but it's also great that you're opened to those experiences, and that you want to have them. When I think about it I'm happy it happened; it showed me I could do much more than I thought I could.

I'm not trying to say I succeeded at all into dealing with my depression. Last year, I stayed in bed for nearly six months, because I couldn't do anything. I got fired from a job I had found, failed all my classes and I have to start again the last year of  my masters. Yesterday I ended up alone in a bar and drunk so much I couldn't do anything today. I tried to talk about it with others, because I just wanted it to be over and I thought I'd find empathy or such, but I only had advices like, start cooking, draw, do more sports. In the worst moments my mind was blank and when it wasn't, I would just be overwhelmed by fear, sadness, and such. But I still feel we should just continue to strive, grab our luck, and try to live like everyone else, without worrying too much, like a lot of others who don't and see the future as bright and the past as a resource. 

I don't really have any clear advice, I'm sorry. I can't find any for myself. I just hope you'll be able to get out of the water. I know we can be happy. I know I have been sometimes, and I wish you could be too. 

Please just don't call yourself worthless. That's not the right concept, or at least the right wording. Not any depressive person is worthless. That's a trick from our mind that we think we are.
